definition: Linear belief functions are an extension of the Dempster–Shafer theory of belief functions to the case when variables of interest are continuous.
details: Examples of such variables include financial asset prices, portfolio performance, and other antecedent and consequent variables. The theory was originally proposed by Arthur P. Dempster in the context of Kalman Filters and later was elaborated, refined, and applied to knowledge representation in artificial intelligence and decision making in finance and accounting by Liping Liu.

explainer.lead: Linear belief functions extend Dempster–Shafer belief functions to continuous variables such as asset prices and portfolio performance. They matter because they bring belief-function reasoning to problems involving continuous quantities rather than discrete hypotheses.

tiers.eli5: Instead of sorting possibilities into labeled buckets, you work with things that vary smoothly, like prices, and still keep track of how confident you are in different ranges.
tiers.practitioner: Used to represent uncertain knowledge over continuous variables in decision-making and finance; a pitfall is that the linear structure limits which dependencies and belief shapes can be represented.
tiers.paperLevel: A Dempster–Shafer belief function generalized to continuous variables; originated in the context of Kalman filters and later refined for knowledge representation and decision making.

explainer.example: Modeling uncertainty about future financial asset prices and portfolio performance as linear belief functions rather than discrete belief masses.
